item.title: Lab 3.1: Can One Attention Head Learn to Look Up an Answer?
item.description:
Lab 3.1: Can One Attention Head Learn to Look Up an Answer?

This is the first LLM internals lab. We’ll open up one operation used in decoder-only Transformers and see whether it can learn to retrieve a value from a prompt. In the Lab 2.3 on LSTMs, information had to travel through each recurrent step. Here the query can directly read from earlier positions.

1. Calculate one attention row by hand

For each position, the query $q_i$ scores the visible keys $k_j$ . Softmax turns those scores into coefficients $a_{ij}$ , and the output is $sum_j a_{ij}v_j$ . The matrices that project inputs into $Q$ , $K$ and $V$ are parameters. The coefficients $a_{ij}$ are recomputed for every input.

item.title: Lab 3.10 — How does a pretrained model adapt?
item.description:
Lab 3.10 — How does a pretrained model adapt?

Continue training the small dense base on uppercase dialogue. This deliberate change makes adaptation measurable using the same character vocabulary. Keep the final tenth of the corpus for evaluation.

Fine-tune on a controlled change

Use 120 batches from a fresh slice of the text. Score uppercase held-out windows before the first update and every twenty updates. Predict what happens to the model’s preference for lowercase continuations.

item.title: Lab 3.11 — Can a rank-four adapter learn the same task?
item.description:
Lab 3.11 — Can a rank-four adapter learn the same task?

Return to the exact pre-adaptation weights. Reuse the full-tuning data, batch order, learning rate and update budget. Change which parameters may move.

Factor the update

For a frozen projection W, use W + BA. A maps input features into four coordinates and B maps those coordinates to output features. Initialize B to zero so the first forward pass matches the base. Which factor gets a nonzero gradient on the very first step?

item.title: Lab 3.12 — Which expert gets the token and the gradient?
item.description:
Lab 3.12 — Which expert gets the token and the gradient?

Branch from the dense Lab 3.9 checkpoint. Replace the final block’s MLP with four equally wide experts. Each token visits one expert. Compare two training runs with exactly the same initial weights and batches.

Route and dispatch

A router produces four probabilities per token. We send the token to its top expert and multiply its output by the selected probability, which lets the task loss train the router. Copy the dense MLP into each expert to control initialization. The gate multiplier changes the initial output even with identical copies.

item.title: Lab 3.2 — From one attention head to a tiny decoder
item.description:
Lab 3.2 — From one attention head to a tiny decoder

Lab 3.1 asked for one answer at the final position. Here every character asks a question. Given everything visible from my position, which character comes next?

1. Turn one line into many predictions

Slide the target one place to the left. For the five-character snippet ROMEO, the inputs are ROME and the targets are OMEO. The row at M can read R, O and M. It gets a reward for assigning probability to E. Teacher forcing supplies the real preceding characters during training. The causal mask lets us score all four rows in one forward pass.

item.title: Lab 3.3 — How does one model produce different continuations?
item.description:
Lab 3.3 — How does one model produce different continuations?

Open the trained character decoder from Lab 3.2. We’ll run it once on ROM, save the last row of logits, and see how many choices we can make from that single row. Only in the last experiment will we feed a chosen character back into the model.

from pathlib import Path
import sys
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import torch
from IPython.display import Image, display
from tiny_decoder import TinyDecoder
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path("../lm-internals").resolve()))
from lm_lab import load_ckpt, save_ckpt
torch.set_num_threads(1)
source = Path("checkpoints/lab32/tiny_decoder.npz")
saved = load_ckpt(source)
alphabet = saved["alphabet"].tolist()
index = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(alphabet)}
limit = int(saved["context_length"])
model = TinyDecoder(len(alphabet), limit, int(saved["width"]))
model.load_state_dict({k: torch.from_numpy(saved[k]) for k in model.state_dict()})
model.eval()
@torch.inference_mode()
def next_logits(prefix):
ids = torch.tensor([[index[ch] for ch in prefix[-limit:]]])
return model(ids)[0, -1]
def leaders(probs, count=3):
values, ids = probs.topk(count)
return [(alphabet[i], round(v.item(), 4)) for v, i in zip(values, ids)]
logits = next_logits("ROM")
base = logits.softmax(0)
print("After ROM:", leaders(base))

After ROM: [('E', 0.6191), ('I', 0.2238), (':', 0.0573)]

1. Stay at one position

Greedy decoding chooses the largest logit. Sampling draws a character with probability proportional to $\exp(z_i/T)$ , where $z_i$ is its logit and $T$ is a positive temperature. Dividing by $T$ changes the gaps between logits. For example, the odds of E relative to I are $\exp((z_E-z_I)/T)$ . Halving the temperature squares those odds.

item.title: Lab 3.4 — When can a decoder reuse its past?
item.description:
Lab 3.4 — When can a decoder reuse its past?

Use the exact Lab 3.2 checkpoint. A cache should change how much work we do while preserving every next-character score. What assumption breaks when the 32-character window slides?

Prefill once, then append

A prefix supplies keys and values at every visible position. One new query only needs its own projection plus those stored rows. Its position index starts at the current cache length. The prefill call still needs a triangular mask because it contains several queries.

item.title: Lab 3.5 — How does text become GPT-2 token IDs?
item.description:
Lab 3.5 — How does text become GPT-2 token IDs?

A character occupied one embedding row in Lab 3.2. Byte-pair encoding (BPE) starts from bytes and learns reusable pieces. Follow one merge before inspecting a real vocabulary.

Train three merges on banana

Count adjacent pairs, merge the most frequent non-overlapping occurrences from left to right, then recount. Ties here follow first occurrence. Predict which pair wins the first tie and how many tokens disappear.

item.title: Lab 3.6 — Can two attention heads fit in one projection?
item.description:
Lab 3.6 — Can two attention heads fit in one projection?

Compute two independent attention maps the slow way, then reproduce them with packed tensors. Both implementations use the same random parameters.

Split the feature axis

With width eight and two heads, each query has four features per head. The softmax runs over source positions separately for each head. Predict the shapes before reading the output.

import torch
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from torch import nn
from llm_lab.experiments import record, show
torch.manual_seed(34)
torch.set_num_threads(1)
from llm_lab.gpt import Attention
head = Attention(8, 2)
x = torch.randn(1, 5, 8)
maps, parts = [], []
q, k, v = head.c_attn(x).chunk(3, -1)
for qi, ki, vi in zip(q.chunk(2,-1), k.chunk(2,-1), v.chunk(2,-1)):
scores = qi @ ki.transpose(-1,-2) / 2
weights = scores.masked_fill(torch.ones(5,5).bool().triu(1), -torch.inf).softmax(-1)
maps.append(weights.detach()[0])
parts.append(weights @ vi)
manual = head.c_proj(torch.cat(parts, -1))
torch.testing.assert_close(manual, head(x))
print("Head maps, joined output:", maps[0].shape, manual.shape)

Head maps, joined output: torch.Size([5, 5]) torch.Size([1, 5, 8])

Remove one head before mixing

The output projection can send each head’s features to every residual coordinate. Predict whether zeroing the first head can change the last four output coordinates. These random heads let us test the algebra without attributing semantic roles to them.

item.title: Lab 3.7 — Where do the parameters in GPT-2 go?
item.description:
Lab 3.7 — Where do the parameters in GPT-2 go?

Assemble a two-block miniature with the same ordering as GPT-2. Read llm_lab/gpt.py alongside the trace. The residual stream keeps its width through every block.

Follow the final token through two blocks

Each block first normalizes its input and adds an attention update. It normalizes the new stream and adds a feedforward update with a fourfold hidden expansion and GELU activation. The final normalization and a dot product with the token embedding table produce vocabulary scores.

item.title: Lab 3.8 — Can our decoder reproduce GPT-2 small?
item.description:
Lab 3.8 — Can our decoder reproduce GPT-2 small?

Load the published GPT-2 small weights into the Lab 3.7 architecture. Compare the same prompt against the Hugging Face implementation at each block boundary in float32 on CPU.

Map the checkpoint

GPT-2 stores its projection matrices in input-by-output order. PyTorch Linear expects output-by-input order. Even the square attention output matrix needs transposing. LayerNorm scales and embedding tables already match. The reference loader below uses the original layout.

item.title: Lab 3.9 — What does one training update do?
item.description:
Lab 3.9 — What does one training update do?

Start with a tiny randomly initialized GPT, check a gradient by two routes, overfit one batch, then train a fresh copy on character windows. The saved base is the common starting point for the next labs.

One batch, two ways to accumulate a gradient

Averaging equally sized microbatch losses gives the full-batch mean. Take one optimizer step only after both backward calls. AdamW tracks first and second gradient moments and applies decoupled weight decay. Watch what happens when it sees the same eight windows repeatedly.

item.title: Decoding Strategies: Greedy, Temperature, Top-k, Top-p, and Beam Search
item.description:
Decoding Strategies: Greedy, Temperature, Top-k, Top-p, and Beam Search

The KV-cache note made the generation loop practical: prefill the prompt, keep each layer’s keys and values, and run only the newest token through the model at every decode step. But it deliberately skipped the final decision in that loop.

After the final Transformer layer and language-model head, we have one logit per vocabulary token. Which token do we actually put into the answer?

item.title: Lab 1.4: Weight Sharing — From Position-Anchored Parts to Convolutional Features
item.description:
Lab 1.4: Weight Sharing — From Position-Anchored Parts to Convolutional Features

MNIST internals series. Lab 1.1 gave us class templates. Lab 1.2 watched them reorganize. Lab 1.3 added a hidden layer and the templates dissolved into shared, position-anchored stroke fragments.

That last phrase is the loose thread. A fully connected hidden unit has a different weight for every pixel, so detecting the same short stroke at two locations costs two different sets of weights. Nothing in the architecture says that a useful pattern in the top-left corner should also be useful in the bottom-right.

item.title: Speculative Decoding: Verifying Several Tokens in Parallel
item.description:
Speculative Decoding: Verifying Several Tokens in Parallel

The decoding-strategies note answered which token to choose from a next-token distribution. It did not remove the central inefficiency of generation: every accepted token normally requires another serial step through the large target model.

KV caching makes each of those steps cheaper by reusing old keys and values. But the loop is still serial:

target model → token 1 → target model → token 2 → target model → token 3

Speculative decoding adds a second, cheaper model called the draft model. The draft proposes several tokens serially. The large target model then examines the whole proposed suffix in one parallel forward pass and decides what to accept.

item.title: KV Cache: Making Autoregressive Generation Practical
item.description:
KV Cache: Making Autoregressive Generation Practical

The language-model training note ended with an asymmetry: training processes every position in parallel, but generation produces one token at a time. Each new token is appended to the context, and the model is run again to predict the next one.

If we implement that loop literally, we repeat an enormous amount of work. To generate token 100, we recompute the embeddings, queries, keys, values, attention outputs, and feedforward outputs for tokens 1 through 99 — even though we already computed all of them in earlier iterations.

item.title: Lab 1.3: From Templates to Features — What One Hidden Layer Does to the Weights
item.description:
Lab 1.3: From Templates to Features — What One Hidden Layer Does to the Weights

MNIST internals series. Lab 1.1 gave us the clean answer: in a linear softmax model, a weight row is a matched-filter photograph of its class. Lab 1.2 showed those photographs being painted, re-carved, and out-bid.

Now the question this series was really building toward: add one hidden layer. What happens to the weight picture?

If you’ve watched 3Blue1Brown’s neural nets series, you might expect: “layers learn edges, then curves, then parts; visualizing raw weights won’t tell you much here.” We can now test that ourselves instead of taking it on faith, and the truth lands in a more interesting place:

item.title: Lab 2.1: How Word Vectors Learn to Mean — Embeddings From Zero, and What They Secretly Compute
item.description:
Lab 2.1: How Word Vectors Learn to Mean — Embeddings From Zero, and What They Secretly Compute

Language-model internals series. In the MNIST series we took apart what weights represent for vision. New series, same ritual — build it from scratch, check gradients numerically, claim nothing without a baseline or a measured number.

The question for this lab, in the plainest possible form:

A word becomes a row of numbers. How can those numbers possibly mean anything?

item.title: Lab 2.2: A Language Model Without Attention — RNN, BPTT, and the Measured Death of Gradient Signal
item.description:
Lab 2.2: A Language Model Without Attention — char-level RNN, backprop through time, and the measured death of gradient signal

Language-model internals series. Lab 2.1 gave words geometry without any sequence at all — windows don’t know order. This lab puts order back, the pre-2017 way: a recurrent network that reads one character at a time and carries everything it remembers in one vector.

The organizing question of this series, sharpened:

item.title: Lab 2.3: Gates as Memory Engineering — LSTM From Scratch on a Task That Was Supposed to Kill the RNN
item.description:
Lab 2.3: Gates as Memory Engineering — LSTM from scratch, on a task that was supposed to kill the RNN

Language-model internals series. Lab 2.2 measured the diagnosis instead of reciting it: on a trained char-RNN, the forward echo of a character and the backward BPTT blame both halve every ~2.3 steps (per-step retention 0.74), because the transported term per step is (roughly) $W_{hh}^{\top}\mathrm{diag}(1-h^2)$ — every step multiplies your memory by something whose average magnitude is far below 1.

item.title: Lab 1.1: MNIST From Pixels to a Neural Network — What Do the Weights Actually Represent?
item.description:
Lab 1.1: What Do the Weights of a Neural Network Actually Represent?

MNIST internals series — the practical companion to the ML notes (softmax & cross-entropy, backprop, training a 2-layer network). This time we stop deriving and start looking.

Anyone who has trained a model eventually asks:

The model is just a pile of numbers. In this lab’s case, exactly 7,860 of them (7,850 weights + 10 biases). What do those numbers actually mean?

item.title: Lab 1.2: Teach It 1s and 2s First, Then Introduce 3 — Watching Weights Reorganize
item.description:
Lab 1.2: Teach It 1s and 2s First, Then Introduce 3 — Watching Weights Reorganize

MNIST internals series. In Lab 1.1 we established what a weight row is: a learned photograph of a class, contrast-carved against its rivals, painted by the update rule $W_c \leftarrow W_c - \eta\,\tfrac1N\sum (\hat p_c - y_c)\,x^\top$ .

Now the experiment that motivated the series: start the model in an impoverished world — only 1s and 2s exist — then let it discover 3. This is continual learning in miniature, and it lets us watch, directly and quantitatively:

item.title: Attention: Turning Token Vectors into Context Vectors
item.description:
Attention: Turning Token Vectors into Context Vectors

The embeddings note ended with an honest limitation: a token’s embedding is one fixed row of a learned matrix. The word “bank” gets the same vector in “river bank” and “investment bank”. Everything the model can possibly know about “bank itself” is frozen into that row at training time.

But meaning is contextual. When a model processes a sentence, what it needs at the position of “bank” is not “the generic bank vector” but “the vector of bank as it appears in this sentence”. Attention is the mechanism that builds that second thing from the first.

item.title: The Transformer Block: Multi-Head Attention, Residuals, Norms, and Position
item.description:
The Transformer Block: Multi-Head Attention, Residuals, Norms, and Position

The attention note derived the single mechanism — softmax over query-key scores, times values — and ended with its two obvious weaknesses: one head can track only one relevance pattern at a time, and the whole operation is blind to token order.

Attention is blind to token order

This was highlighted in previous note here

4. Sets, not sequences. Nothing in the formula knows which token came first. Permute the input rows of $X$ and the outputs permute identically — attention is permutation equivariant: it treats the sequence as a bag of tokens with affinities. That’s great for set-like inputs and a true bug for language, whose meaning is bound up in order (“dog bites man” ≠ “man bites dog”). Fixing that is positional encoding, coming in the next note.

One attention head can learn only relevance pattern at a time

This idea was only mentioned at the end of the previous note. It was never justified or derived.

So let’s try to make sense of it.

Short answer: The answer lies in what happens when we compute $QK^\top$ . From 3b1b’s video if this token is useful to another token, what information should it send? If we think about it, a token can be useful to the next token in multiple different ways—for a given token A, its predecessor token B might be more useful when considering grammatical context, and token C might be more useful when considering semantic context. We are forcing one attention head to somehow capture all those relationships and turn them into one set of weights ( $W_Q$ , $W_K$ , and $W_V$ ). Even if it somehow ends up capturing these different spatial relationships, at best they fight with each other and average them out.

(Technically, $W_V$ (the Value weights) doesn’t decide who to look at; it only decides what information to extract once the connection is made. The “fighting and averaging out” happens specifically inside $W_Q$ and $W_K$ , which calculate the attention map.)

Long answer:

One attention head can only learn one relevance pattern at a time because the query-key interaction is governed by a single pair of linear projection matrices ( $W_Q$ and $W_K$ ).

When we compute $QK^\top$ , we perform a single matrix multiplication that collapses the high-dimensional token representations into one scalar affinity score for every pair of tokens. Mathematically and conceptually, here is why this limits a single head to one “type” of similarity:

item.title: Training a Language Model End to End: From Text to Loss to Generation
item.description:
Training a Language Model End to End: From Text to Loss to Generation

We now have every moving part: token → embedding (the lookup note), tokens mix via masked multi-head attention (previous two notes), blocks stack, and the whole thing is just a computation graph built from matrix multiplies and softmax — the exact family the general $L$ -layer loop handles.

What remains is boring-sounding but is actually the point of the whole series: how does a stack of transformer blocks become a language model that predicts text? The answer has four pieces: a final linear layer to vocabulary-sized logits, cross-entropy per position against the next token, teacher forcing during training, and autoregressive sampling at inference. The pieces are individually simple; seeing them end-to-end is what makes “GPT” stop being magical.

item.title: Activation Functions: Why Sigmoid Fades and ReLU Won
item.description:
Activation Functions: Why Sigmoid Fades and ReLU Won

The previous note finished with pseudocode for a network of any depth $L$ . One line in that pseudocode deserved more attention:

dZ[l-1] = dA[l-1] * activation_derivative(A[l-1])

Everything else in the backward pass is matrix multiplication — copying, scaling, and adding error signals. This one line is different: it is the only place where the network’s non-linearity touches the gradients. The choice of activation function decides whether error signals survive the trip from output back to input, or die on the way.

item.title: Embeddings: From One-Hot Vectors to Learned Representations
item.description:
Embeddings: From One-Hot Vectors to Learned Representations

Everything in the previous notes assumed the network’s input was already a list of numbers — x1 = 1, x2 = 2, pixel intensities, whatever. But most interesting data is not numeric. “cat”, “dog”, “bank”, user IDs, product IDs, words of a sentence. Neural networks cannot multiply the string "cat" by a weight matrix. Somewhere between the raw symbol and the first linear layer, a translation to numbers must happen, and the way we do it — the embedding layer — turns out to be one of the most consequential ideas in modern deep learning.

item.title: Softmax and Multiclass Cross-Entropy: Turning Raw Scores Into Probabilities
item.description:
Softmax and Multiclass Cross-Entropy: Turning Raw Scores Into Probabilities

So far, every classification in these notes has been binary — spam or not, XOR’s 0 or 1 — and the output has been single sigmoid feeding binary cross-entropy, whose gradient collapsed to the beautiful $\delta = a - y$ .

Real classifiers rarely answer two-way questions. “Which of 10 digits is this image?” “Which of 50,000 tokens comes next?” “Is this a cat, a dog, or a bird?” This note generalizes the output of a neural network to $k$ classes, and it turns out almost everything we know carries over — with soft-max doing the job sigmoid did.

item.title: Training a 2-Layer Network in NumPy: From Scalar to Vectorized Backprop
item.description:
Training a 2-Layer Network in NumPy: From Scalar to Vectorized Backprop

The previous note did the backward pass for a small 2-layer network by hand, one scalar at a time. That is the best way to understand what backprop actually does.

This note takes the next step: turn that scalar walk into compact, vectorized NumPy code. The math is unchanged; the only thing that changes is notation. I will introduce every matrix slowly — what its rows and columns mean, where the division by the batch size comes from, and why it is exactly the same algorithm you already did by hand.

item.title: Backpropagation in a Fully-Connected Network, From Scratch
item.description:
• Why is there no deadlock in the order of corrections?
  • Why is this cheap enough to do for billions of parameters?
  • What is PyTorch’s autograd doing when you call loss.backward()?

1. What you will learn

  • The shape of a fully-connected (dense) network and what “fully-connected” means.
  • How to forward a single training example through every operation, by hand.
  • The backward pass as a message-passing process, with the exact algebra at each edge.
  • The recursion that lets you go from 2 layers to 100 layers.
  • Why nothing breaks due to ordering — the backward pass computes gradients; it does not apply updates.
  • Why backprop costs about one extra forward pass, not one forward pass per parameter.
  • A pseudocode implementation of the whole algorithm.
  • What an autograd engine records, and how loss.backward() / optimizer.step() / optimizer.zero_grad() map onto what we do by hand.

2. The network we are going to train

Logistic regression is a single layer: input → weighted sum → sigmoid → probability. Its decision boundary is a line (or hyperplane). There is a famous class of problems it cannot solve — XOR is the classic example — where no single line separates the two classes.

item.title: Computational Graphs, Part 2: Branching — Why Gradients Add
item.description:
Computational Graphs, Part 2: Branching — Why Gradients Add

The previous note covered the forward pass, the chain rule, and the backward pass on a graph where every input had exactly one path to the output. This note adds the one remaining piece: what happens when an input feeds into more than one operation.

When that happens, there are multiple paths from the input to the output. The chain rule tells us to add the contributions from those paths.

item.title: Computational Graphs, Part 3: A Single Neuron and Logistic Regression
item.description:
Computational Graphs, Part 3: A Single Neuron and Logistic Regression

The previous note showed how gradients add when one input feeds multiple operations. With that in place, we can now look at a real model: a single neuron. We will draw it as a graph, run the forward pass and backward pass by hand, and then connect it back to the logistic regression from the first note.

1. What you will learn

  • How a single neuron is a small computational graph.
  • The forward pass through a weighted sum and an activation function.
  • The backward pass through the same graph.
  • Why logistic regression is exactly a one-neuron network with sigmoid activation.
  • How the cross-entropy loss fits into the graph as an extra node.
  • Why the gradient formula from logistic regression matches the chain-rule result.

item.title: Computational Graphs and Backpropagation
item.description:
Computational Graphs and Backpropagation

This note explains how to compute gradients for any function by breaking it into a graph of simple operations. It is the bridge between the gradient-descent picture from the linear and logistic regression note and the layered functions we will later call neural networks.

The ideas are:

  1. Draw the function as a graph of operations.
  2. Evaluate the graph from inputs to output: the forward pass.
  3. Use the chain rule to carry sensitivities from the output back to the inputs: the backward pass.

We build this on one tiny example and walk through every step.

item.title: ML Refresher: Linear and Logistic Regression
item.description:
ML Refresher: Linear and Logistic Regression

This is the first note in the ML → Deep Learning → Transformers → LLMs series. The goal is to rebuild working memory of the basics before we get to neural networks: what a model is, how a loss function measures error, and how gradient descent tunes parameters.

We will implement linear regression and logistic regression from scratch in NumPy, then compare with scikit-learn. If the code and gradients feel obvious, you are ready for the next note (computational graphs and backprop). If not, this is exactly the foundation to lock down first.
